catalog_quote: Kayan languages also have penultimate stress, but actively shift stress to the final syllable if the penult is a schwa (Clayre and Cubit 1974 for Baram River Kayan; Smith 2017a for Data Dian Kayan, spoken in Indonesia). [...] In the dialect of Kayan spoken in Data Dian gemination is observed after a penultimate schwa but not after other vowels (Smith 2017a). As noted earlier in §3.2.2, Kayan usually has penultimate stress, but, in examples with a schwa in the penult, stress is word-final. [...] (19) Data Dian Kayan (Smith 2018b) təpaʔ [təpːáʔ] 'pound rice' səpun [səpːún] 'great grandparent', mətaŋ [mətːáŋ] 'ask' dənaʔ [dənːáʔ] 'slow'

new_statements.relation_note: Penultimate stress by default; stress shifts to the final syllable when the penult contains schwa, with gemination of the following onset (təpaʔ [təpːáʔ] etc.).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable; if the penult nucleus is schwa (analysed as weightless), stress falls on the final syllable and the final-syllable onset geminates.
new_statements.exceptions: schwa penult -> final stress (with onset gemination); no lexical exceptions mentioned
new_statements.identity_note: Data Dian is on the Kayan River (Kec. Peso area, Bulungan); Glottolog/GROUP alt names list 'Data Dian Kayan (Smith)' = Kayan River Kayan xkn; data from Smith's own fieldwork (Smith 2017a diss., Smith 2018b ADS2-001). [name in source: Data Dian Kayan ('the dialect of Kayan spoken in Data Dian', 'spoken in Indonesia'); pages sec. 3.2.2 (author p. [14]) and sec. 4.2.1 with ex. (19) (p. [26]); journal pagination 111-152]

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2013. The Austronesian languages (rev. ed.), sec. 4.3 (Borneo). Asia-Pacific Linguistics Open Access Monographs 8. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: General Borneo statement only, not Kayan-specific: 'Unlike the Philippines, stress is not phonemic in any language of Borneo. However, unlike much of the AN world, where stress falls predictably on the penult, many of the languages of coastal Sarawak, and some interior languages have final stress in citation forms, but penultimate stress in phrasal context.'

sources.citation: Blust, Robert A. 1977. Sketches of the morphology and phonology of Bornean languages 1: Uma Juman (Kayan). In Papers in Borneo and Western Austronesian Linguistics No. 2, 9-122. Pacific Linguistics A-33. Canberra: ANU.https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/handle/1885/254321
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in
sources.note: SISTER LANGUAGE ONLY (Uma Juman = Rejang Kayan [ree] reja1241, Balui basin, Sarawak; not xkn). Rule 8 'stress placement', printed p. 76 (p. 69 of the chapter file): 'In citation forms the last vowel of a word receives stress. Stress is penultimate within the phrase.' Also p. 33 (general): stress final in citation forms but penultimate in context 'in most of the languages described'; p. 24: affixes not normally stressed, full words bear stress; p. 85: locative clitic /ha?/ never stressed in rapid speech.

Read the whole text for Kayan/Kayanic/Borneo and all stress passages. The paper contains NO prose statement of the Kayan stress rule. Its only Kayan-specific content is example (1c), p. 343: two Data Dian Kayan forms cited from Smith 2018 (Kaipuleohone Kayanic vocabularies) transcribed with gemination of the final-syllable onset after penultimate schwa and an acute (stress) on the FINAL vowe…

sources.citation: Smith, Alexander D. 2017. Merap historical phonology in the context of a central Bornean linguistic area. Oceanic Linguistics 56(1): 143-180. doi:10.1353/ol.2017.0006
sources.note: No stress statement for Kayan; all stress statements concern Merap ('stress appears regularly on the final syllable') and the eight 'central Bornean linguistic area' languages (Sa'ban, Kiput, Gaai, Kelai, Modang, Long Gelat, Hliboi, Oma Longh) that 'independently shifted stress to the final syllable'; the Kayan group is called 'phonologically conservative'.

sources.citation: Guerreiro, Antonio J. 1996. Homophony, sound changes and dialectal variations in some central Bornean languages. Mon-Khmer Studies 25: 205-226.
sources.note: Nothing on stress in any Kayan variety. It names the xkn groups (Uma' Lekan, Uma' Laran, Uma' Lasan; Apo Kayan) in lexical comparisons and lists Kayanic phonological traits (diphthongization, vowel clusters, 'lengthening of vowels in open syllables', gemination, p. ~210); the only 'unstressed' remark (p. 212) is Haudricourt's general claim about vowel dropping applied to Modang.
